title: Alcohol and Arthritis: Evidence, Medicines and Safety
meta_title: Alcohol and Arthritis: Evidence, Medicines and Safety
meta_description: Alcohol and arthritis: mixed research, UK units, medicine-specific cautions and help to cut down safely. No reason to start drinking for joint health.
excerpt: Alcohol and arthritis: mixed research, UK units, medicine-specific cautions and help to cut down safely. No reason to start drinking for joint health.
direct_answer: Do not start drinking alcohol to treat arthritis. Research is mixed and does not prove that alcohol improves rheumatoid arthritis. UK low-risk guidance is no more than 14 units a week regularly, but medicines and health conditions may mean less or none. Get medical help before cutting down if you have withdrawal symptoms.
author: Louis Maxwell
keywords: alcohol arthritis, drinking with arthritis UK
content:
Quick answer: Do not start drinking alcohol to treat arthritis. Research linking drinking with rheumatoid arthritis symptoms is mixed and does not prove that alcohol improves the disease. If you drink, UK low-risk guidance is no more than 14 units a week on a regular basis, but your medicines, liver health and other circumstances may mean a lower limit or no alcohol. If you get withdrawal symptoms when you cut down, get medical help before changing your drinking.

Does alcohol help or harm arthritis?

There is no single answer for every type of arthritis, and feeling temporarily more relaxed after a drink is not evidence that joint inflammation or damage has improved. Alcohol is not an arthritis treatment. Keep following the treatment plan agreed with your healthcare team.

Rheumatoid arthritis: why the headlines disagree

Some observational studies have found lower disease activity or better quality of life among people with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) who drink. For example, a 2023 Swedish study following 1,228 people with newly diagnosed RA found this association and argued that changes in drinking because of illness did not fully explain it. The study relied on self-reported drinking and outcomes, and included few heavy drinkers.

Other research reaches a different conclusion. A longitudinal study of changes in alcohol use found no clear benefit for disease activity after accounting for factors that influence whether people drink. Poorer health can lead people to stop drinking, making non-drinkers and drinkers different before the comparison begins.

A systematic review informing EULAR lifestyle recommendations reported associations between moderate or higher alcohol intake and flares in RA and gout, while stressing the limitations of observational evidence. These studies do not establish that starting alcohol treats RA, or that stopping it will worsen RA. Discuss your own symptoms and drinking with your rheumatology team rather than using a headline as a prescription.

Gout: drinking less is not a replacement for treatment

NICE advises that excessive alcohol can worsen gout flares and symptoms. It also says there is not enough evidence that any specific diet prevents flares or lowers blood urate, so it recommends a healthy, balanced diet. This is not a reason to rely on dietary changes alone.

The NHS gout guide identifies drinking too much alcohol and dehydration as possible triggers. Keep taking prescribed uric-acid-lowering medicine regularly, including when symptoms settle. If you have repeated attacks, or usual treatment is not helping, ask your GP for a review.

Osteoarthritis and other joint conditions

Do not turn findings about RA into advice for knee or hip osteoarthritis, psoriatic arthritis or every cause of joint pain. The EULAR evidence review found limited and differing evidence across conditions. A personal discussion should consider your diagnosis, medicines and overall health, not just whether a drink seems to change pain that evening.

What does the UK 14-unit guidance mean?

The NHS low-risk drinking guidance advises men and women not to drink more than 14 units a week on a regular basis. If you regularly drink as much as 14 units, spread it over three or more days and try to have several drink-free days. Do not save the weekly amount for one evening.

This is a low-risk limit, not a target or a guarantee of safety with medicines. There is no completely safe level of drinking. Drinking less reduces alcohol-related health risks. If you are pregnant or think you could become pregnant, the NHS advises not drinking alcohol as the safest approach. If you have possible alcohol dependence, seek medical help before stopping or reducing, including before trying drink-free days.

A glass is not a unit

NHS guidance calculates units from the drink's volume and strength: millilitres multiplied by the ABV percentage, divided by 1,000. Check the actual label or ask staff, because servings and strengths vary.

  • A 175 ml glass of wine at 12% ABV contains 2.1 units.
  • A 500 ml beer at 5% ABV contains 2.5 units.
  • A 25 ml spirit measure at 40% ABV contains 1 unit; a larger measure contains more.

These are worked examples, not recommended servings or a way to calculate when it is safe to drive.

Check the medicine, not just the arthritis diagnosis

Bring your prescription list, bought medicines and supplements to a pharmacist or your rheumatology team. Tell them how much you actually drink, including occasional heavier sessions. Do not skip, move or reduce prescribed doses to make room for alcohol.

Methotrexate and leflunomide

The NHS methotrexate page says alcohol is usually OK with a low weekly dose of 25 mg or less used long term for an inflammatory condition, and advises people taking high doses to ask their doctor. That is not personal clearance to drink up to 14 units, and it does not cover every liver condition or medicine combination.

NRAS explains that both methotrexate and leflunomide can affect the liver. Ask your team what limit applies to you, particularly if liver blood tests have changed, you have liver disease, or you take more than one medicine that affects the liver. Keep attending monitoring appointments and be honest about recent drinking so results can be interpreted properly. This guide does not set a drinking allowance for leflunomide.

Anti-inflammatory painkillers

The NHS says drinking a lot of alcohol with NSAIDs, such as ibuprofen or naproxen, may increase side effects or irritate the stomach. NSAIDs can also cause ulcers and bleeding. A weekly alcohol limit does not remove an individual's stomach or bleeding risk. Ask a pharmacist about the exact product, dose, other medicines and your history.

Codeine and medicines that make you sleepy

The NHS advises that it is best not to drink alcohol with codeine, because it increases side-effect risk. Check combination products too, including codeine mixed with another painkiller. Codeine can cause serious breathing problems.

Alcohol can make amitriptyline-related sleepiness worse; the NHS advises avoiding alcohol until you know how the medicine affects you. Other sedating medicines need their own check. Do not drive or use tools if you feel sleepy or dizzy, and ask for advice rather than assuming a small drink is harmless.

A practical plan that does not depend on willpower alone

First, check for withdrawal risk. If you shake, sweat, feel sick or feel anxious until you have a drink, ask a GP or alcohol support service for medical help before cutting down. The suggestions below are not a withdrawal or detox plan.

  • Count what you drink. Write down the volume and ABV rather than just the number of glasses. Take that record to a medicine review.
  • Choose the occasion. If it is appropriate for you to reduce without medical supervision, try a smaller serving, a lower-strength option or a soft drink. Check labels rather than assuming a product has no alcohol.
  • Keep the social part. Suggest breakfast, a film or a coffee instead of rounds of drinks. You do not owe anyone a detailed explanation of your medicines.
  • Make a plan for difficult days. If drinking is becoming a way to cope with pain, sleep or worry, tell your GP or rheumatology team. Ask for help with the underlying problem as well as alcohol use.

The NHS Drink less page offers tools and support, including Drinkline on 0300 123 1110 for free, confidential advice about your own or someone else's drinking. Your GP or a local alcohol service can help you find treatment. You do not need to wait until things feel out of control to ask.

When to get medical help

NHS alcohol-use disorder guidance warns that suddenly stopping can be dangerous if you are dependent. Get medical help before stopping or reducing if you get withdrawal symptoms. Do not use an online taper or this article to manage withdrawal yourself.

Call 999 or go to A&E for severe alcohol withdrawal symptoms, such as visible shaking, confusion, hallucinations or a seizure. Do not drive yourself. Call 999 if you suspect alcohol poisoning, including if someone loses consciousness or has slow or irregular breathing.

A hot, swollen or suddenly very painful joint should not automatically be put down to drinking or gout. NHS septic arthritis guidance advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for sudden severe joint pain, swelling, skin colour change or difficulty moving the joint, particularly if you feel unwell or shivery. Fever is not always present.

Should I start drinking red wine for my joints?

No. Observational links do not establish an arthritis treatment benefit. There is no need to start drinking for joint health, and alcohol has health risks beyond arthritis.

Can I miss a methotrexate dose for a night out?

Do not skip or change prescribed treatment to drink. Ask your rheumatology team or pharmacist about your medicine, blood tests and the advice that applies to you.

Does 14 units mean alcohol is safe for me?

No. It is general low-risk guidance, not personal clearance. Your medicine, liver health, pregnancy or dependence risk may require different advice. If you have withdrawal symptoms, get medical help before reducing.

Sources checked for this editorial revision on 19 November 2026. Fresh qualified clinical review remains pending. This is general information, not a personal drinking allowance or withdrawal plan.
